doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: Identifying Bill Watrous and their relationship
summary: Fedchock recognizes Watrous on a recording, recounts the Leonard Feather article, his thank-you letter and Watrous's phone call.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: All right. I’m going to play a couple of things here. This is from one of, I guess you could call it one of your contemporaries.
Unmistakable within the first couple of measures, that was Bill Watrous.
First of all I appreciate you considering me one of his contemporaries, but Bill’s like 20 years older than me and has had a glorious career.
It’s still alive, which is great.

Yeah. And I’ve had some wonderful opportunities to hang out with him and play music with him and talk with him on the phone and he was very supportive of me early on. During my days with Woody Herman I know I still have a copy of it — there was an interview with him — Leonard Feather did an interview with him in the L.A. Times and when Leonard Feather asked him about new people coming up and he mentioned me and my writing and all that. And I was in New York and someone sent me the article and I saw it and I said wow this is amazing. So I wrote him a letter, not thinking anything, I

just wrote him a letter, “thank you so much you’ve been a big influence over the years.” And he called me up. Out of the blue. Like shocking. I’d never met him before. So a really good guy and unbelievable technique. And when I was in high school was when his first big band records were coming out. And it was super-inspirational. Because kind of like Woody Herman with all the young guys, his group was kind of doing more like modern kind of Latin music and contemporary rock and things like that that were not really done with a lot of the older big bands. And of course all featuring trombone. How could I not like that? So he was one of my early influences in high school. My first one was Urbie Green but Bill definitely — that first big band album I got of his, the Wildlife — Manhattan Wildlife Refuge — when he does his crazy cadenza on this one tune that, how does anybody have that much technique. Unbelievable.
Yeah. I remember watching in college a rare video, well before, you know YouTube wasn’t thought of, but just watching this guy play with the Prince Valiant haircut and like.
